description: Team Silica is building a lunar survival game for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. We aim to combine coding, creativity, and space science to explore life on the Moon. We're looking for teammates interested in software, game development, design, data analysis, or space science. Bring your ideas and let's build together!
summary: Silica Station is a browser-based lunar survival game that turns authentic NASA data into a playable mission trainer for students. Players guide a crew through 12 escalating survival decisions, balancing power, repairs, communication, and crew health while each choice creates consequences that surface several rounds later. The game uses live or recorded NASA space-weather and radiation data to shape the mission briefing and influence in-game flare risk, making real scientific conditions part of the gameplay rather than background decoration. This addresses the challenge of making complex space science engaging, understandable, and relevant for younger audiences. It is important because it teaches how astronauts make high-stakes decisions under uncertainty, highlights the real impact of solar storms and radiation, and shows how NASA data can be transformed into an accessible, memorable educational experience that inspires interest in STEM and space exploration.
details:
Silica Station is a browser-based lunar survival game and mission trainer designed to make space science understandable, engaging, and memorable for younger learners.

Players take on the role of a junior astronaut managing a lunar base through 12 escalating rounds of decision-making. Each choice affects crew health, power, repairs, communication, and mission stability, and the consequences are intentionally delayed so players experience how small actions can compound into larger problems later. The game is built around a “systems thinking” model: players must balance short-term survival with long-term risk, making decisions under uncertainty while adapting to changing conditions.

The project stands out because it uses real NASA data as part of the gameplay rather than as a static fact panel. Each day, the system can fetch or replay a mission briefing based on live or recorded space-weather and radiation data from NASA sources, including DONKI and related datasets. That information influences the scenario and creates mission events such as solar flare risk, making the science behind space travel visible in the game itself. This adds authenticity and helps players understand why radiation and space weather matter on lunar missions. It also supports replayability, because the game can pin a “same scenario” run to a specific NASA snapshot and compare outcomes across players.

The benefits are both educational and practical: students learn about mission planning, risk assessment, and space systems while developing decision-making and problem-solving skills. The project is intended to make STEM learning more accessible and inspiring, especially for younger audiences who may not engage with science through traditional classroom formats. We developed it using TypeScript, React, Vite, Zustand, Express, SQLite, and Vitest, with a backend that stores anonymous runs, verifies game outcomes, and serves NASA data safely and clearly. The creative aspect comes from combining gameplay mechanics, narrative storytelling, and authentic scientific data into a single experience. Our team considered accessibility, kid-friendly communication, scientific accuracy, privacy, replay verification, and fairness so the project would be both educationally valuable and trustworthy.
